t: Swap For Longest Repeated Character Substring — Grouped Runs and Sliding Window
o: We may perform exactly one swap of any two characters in `text`, then want the longest run of a single repeated character. A swap is only useful if it brings in one extra copy of some character c from elsewhere in the string. So for each character we care about its maximal blocks (runs) of consecutive occurrences: either we extend a block by 1 (if another copy of c exists outside it), or we merge two adjacent blocks separated by exactly one different character (if enough copies of c exist overall). For "ababa", the 'a' blocks are lengths 1,1,1; merging the first two through the single 'b' gives 3. For "aaabaaa", blocks are 3 and 3 around one 'b'; merging needs an extra 'a' outside, giving 6. With n up to 2·10^4, both an O(n) grouping pass and a sliding window work comfortably.
k: Only runs of identical characters matter; compress text into (char, count) blocks.
Answer per character = max(block length + 1 if spare copy exists, merged length of two blocks separated by one char when total count allows).
A sliding window with at most one 'foreign' character inside achieves the same result without explicit grouping.

a.i: Compress the string into consecutive blocks like [(c, len), ...]. For each block of character c of length L, candidate L+1 if count[c] > L (there is a spare c to swap in). For each pair of adjacent blocks of the same character c separated by exactly one other block, candidate len1 + len2 (+1 if count[c] > len1+len2, else just len1+len2 by swapping the separator away). Take the maximum over all candidates.
s: Scan text once building blocks (char, length); also record total count of each character.
For each block, consider length + 1 if count[char] exceeds the block length.
For each i where blocks[i-1] and blocks[i+1] have the same char c, consider their sum plus 1 if count[c] > that sum.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to build blocks plus one pass over them.
a.sp: O(n) for the blocks list (at most n blocks).

a.n: Approach 2: Sliding Window with One Foreign Character
a.i: The best window after one swap contains at most one character different from the majority character inside it. Maintain a sliding window whose count of non-majority characters is at most 1; such a window can always be turned into a full run of its majority character via one swap, provided a spare copy exists outside (checked against total counts). Track the best valid window length.
s: Count total frequency of each character.
Slide right pointer, incrementing counts; track the max frequency inside the window.
While window length minus maxFreq exceeds 1, shrink from the left.
Candidate answer is min(window length, total count of the majority char): the swap must supply the missing character from outside.
a.t: O(26·n) ≈ O(n) — each character enters/leaves the window once; recomputing the max over 26 letters is constant factor.

w: In an interview, lead with the sliding-window framing since it generalizes to 'at most k swaps' easily; the block-grouping approach is more direct for exactly one swap and slightly faster in practice. Pitfalls: forgetting the spare-copy check (e.g., "aaabaaa" must not answer 7), forgetting that merging two blocks without a spare copy still yields len1+len2 (swap the separator out), and handling single-character strings. Edge cases: all same characters (answer n), no repeats at all (answer 1). Follow-ups: generalize to k swaps (window allowing k foreign chars), or return the actual swapped string.
